title: Reminiscences and regrets
subtitle: think back, what became of, rue the day, pangs of guilt
summary: Talk about the past the way native speakers do - reminiscing, losing touch, seeing things through rose-tinted spectacles - and express regret at every level of formality.

lesson.heading: Looking back: sharing memories
lesson.text: Two old schoolfriends meet after ten years. *A:* Gosh, it's ten years since we were at school together! Any idea what the school is like these days? *B:* No, I've been a bit **out of touch** with things ever since I moved away from London. To be **out of touch** is not to know what has happened recently, and if you **lose touch with** someone you stop hearing from them.

examples.text: I wonder what **became of** that maths teacher.
examples.note: became of = happened to; where he is now

examples.text: I think his name, **if I recall**, was Mr Sanderson.
examples.note: if I recall = if I remember correctly

examples.text: Do you ever **hear anything of** James?
examples.note: hear anything of = receive any news about

examples.text: I often wonder what Sanjay ended up doing. I've **lost touch** with him too.

lesson.heading: Thinking back
lesson.text: **Think back** and **look back** both mean to think about the past. The -ing forms are very common at the start of a sentence: **Thinking back, ...** / **When I look back, ...**

examples.text: When I **think back**, I realise now how difficult things must have been for him.
**Thinking back**, we had some great times, didn't we?
When I **look back**, I realise how much things have changed.

lesson.heading: When something triggers a memory
rows: remind someone of
make someone remember
Seeing your phone reminds me of how we used to text under our desks.
take someone back to
make someone remember a particular time
That takes me back to the day my phone rang in class.
have a vague memory of
have a memory that is not very clear
I have a vague memory of that.
it's all coming back to me
I am beginning to remember it more clearly
Actually, it's all coming back to me now - they confiscated your phone!
stand/stick out in my mind
be what I remember more than other things
What stands out in my mind is the amazing freedom we used to have.
lesson.note: Do not confuse remind and remember: Seeing the class photo again reminded me of my unhappy schooldays - not ~~remembered me~~.

lesson.heading: Reminiscing and nostalgia
lesson.text: To **reminisce about** something is to think or talk about pleasant things that happened in the past. **Nostalgia** is the feeling of pleasure, and sometimes slight sadness, that goes with it. If you look at the past **through rose-tinted spectacles**, you see only the pleasant things and ignore the unpleasant ones.

examples.text: I often find myself **reminiscing about** my teenage years.
We all tend to look at the past **through rose-tinted spectacles**, don't we?
examples.note: you can also say rose-coloured spectacles

examples.text: A bit of **nostalgia** does nobody any harm!
I got a sudden feeling of **nostalgia** as we drove past our old house.

lesson.heading: Expressing regret
lesson.text: **Regret** is normally followed by an -ing form. **Remorse** is a strong feeling of regret for something bad you have done, and **shame** is embarrassment and guilt about something bad that happened. **Pangs** are sudden sharp feelings, especially of painful emotion.

examples.text: I **regret not spending** more time with my aunt when she was ill.
He showed no sign of **remorse** for what he had done.
She said she felt great **shame** for what had happened and apologised to us all.
I felt great **pangs of guilt** and remorse thinking of all the bad things that had happened.
examples.note: pangs collocates with guilt, regret, conscience, remorse

lesson.heading: Formal, rather literary ways of expressing regret
rows: rue
regret very much (collocates strongly with 'the day' and 'the fact that')
I rue the day we ever met.
lament
feel sad about something
I lament the passing of time.
mourn
feel sad about something you have lost
I mourn my lost opportunities.

lesson.text: A thing reminds you of something; you remember the thing itself. Never say 'it remembered me'.

exercises.prompt: ___ back, I can't believe how I survived the first day in my old job. It was horrendous.
exercises.explanation: Looking back / Thinking back both mean thinking about the past.

exercises.prompt: What ___ out in my mind when I think of my schooldays was our class trip to Edinburgh.
exercises.explanation: What stands out / sticks out in your mind is what you remember more than anything else.

exercises.prompt: What ___ of that friend of yours who wanted to be a pilot? Did he ever get to be one?
exercises.explanation: What became of someone? asks where they are now and what happened to them.

exercises.prompt: Do you ever hear ___ your old college friend Martine these days?
exercises.explanation: To hear anything of someone is to receive any news about them.

exercises.prompt: When I get together with my old schoolmates, we often ___ about the fun times we had.
exercises.hint: (think or talk about the pleasant past)
exercises.explanation: To reminisce about something is to think or talk about pleasant past events.

exercises.prompt: I'm a bit out of ___ with what's happening with our old hockey team since I stopped playing.
exercises.hint: (out of ___ = not knowing the latest news)
exercises.explanation: To be out of touch with something is not to know what has happened recently.

exercises.prompt: When I saw the photo, it all ___ back to me just what a wonderful holiday we had had.
exercises.explanation: It's all coming back to me means I am beginning to remember it more clearly.

exercises.prompt: You're always looking at the past through rose-___ spectacles. It wasn't all wonderful, you know.
exercises.explanation: To see things through rose-tinted (or rose-coloured) spectacles is to notice only the pleasant side.

exercises.prompt: I have only a very ___ memory of my early childhood in Canada. It was all so long ago!
exercises.explanation: A vague memory is one that is not very clear.

exercises.prompt: What happened to your sister? If I ___ , she wanted to study chemistry, didn't she?
exercises.explanation: If I recall means if I remember correctly.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginning of each sentence about regret with its ending.

pairs.right: I agreed to go into business with him.
about what happened. It was my fault.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite more formally: 'I'm sorry that I didn't buy her a birthday present.' I ___ buying her a birthday present.
exercises.explanation: Regret is followed by an -ing form: I regret not buying her a present.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite more formally: 'They didn't seem the least bit concerned about what they had done.' They showed no ___ for what they had done.
exercises.explanation: To show no remorse is to show no regret for something bad you have done.

exercises.prompt: Which is the formal, literary way to say 'The whole village felt sad about the loss of the beautiful trees'?
options: The whole village mourned the loss of the beautiful trees.
The whole village reminisced the loss of the beautiful trees.
The whole village recalled the loss of the beautiful trees.
The whole village rued the trees.
exercises.explanation: To mourn something is to feel sad about something you have lost.

exercises.statement: Seeing the class photo again remembered me of my unhappy schooldays.
exercises.explanation: Seeing the class photo again reminded me of my unhappy schooldays. Things remind you; you remember them.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression about remembering the past, or about regretting it?
